newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian media told not to poll or predict election.
newsitem.headline: Zambian media told not to poll or predict election.

text.p: Media organisations in Zambia reacted angrily on Thursday to new regulations introduced by the government to control election coverage, saying they would hamper reporting of a general election set for November 18.
Some independent newspapers said they would defy the regulations which ban broadcasters and publishers from speculating on the elections outcome or conducting opinion polls.

The government of President Frederick Chiluba, in office for five years, is seeking a fresh mandate from voters. Some opposition parties are boycotting the election and several candidates have been excluded by new laws.

Chiluba's government has been criticised by aid donors to Zambia for its law preventing non-Zambians from running for office -- a highly controversial piece of legislation apparently aimed at excluding former president Kenneth Kaunda, the country's best-known politician.
Journalists who defy the election reporting regulations will be liable to three months' imprisonment, according to authorities.

"We will continue writing on elections, basing our stories on international standards and not on standards set by a bunch of ignorant people who do not even consult those they want to regulate. They can go to hell," the managing editor of The Post, Fred Mmembe, said.

The Monitor, a weekly set up to report on the electoral proccess, described the regulations as an attempt to muzzle the strident independent press, which has been critical of the organisation of the general election.
"I am afraid we will have to defy the regulations if it happens that they hamper our work," said news editor Elias Chitenje.
Opposition parties urged the media to ignore the order.
"You have a right to express yourself under the constitution and no one can take that right away from you," prominent lawyer and Liberal Progressive Front leader Rodger Chongwe said.

Electoral commission chairman Judge Bobby Bwalya defended the rules and said "they were made merely to ensure that people who do not know anything about elections desist from making wild statements about them."
